_about: Hand-written country stories, keyed by ISO code. Shape: hook (one line, never the country's name) · land · people · surprise · scale (everyday comparisons) · sources · checks (numbers the tests verify against the World Bank data) · status (sample | draft | reviewed).

BTN.hook: The country that breathes in more carbon than it breathes out.
BTN.land: Bhutan climbs from steamy jungle about 100 m above the sea to Himalayan ice above 7,000 m, all in less than 200 km. That's every climate on Earth in one long bus ride.
BTN.people: About 8 lakh people live mostly in the river valleys in between. The forests are protected by the constitution itself: at least 60% of the land must stay forest, forever.
BTN.surprise: Gangkhar Puensum (7,570 m) is the highest mountain nobody has ever climbed. Bhutan doesn't allow it: the big peaks are home to the gods, and the gods like their privacy.
BTN.scale: About the size of Kerala, with fewer people than Chandigarh. India could hold 85 Bhutans.
sources: Constitution of the Kingdom of Bhutan (2008), Article 5

ISL.hook: An island that's slowly being pulled in two.
ISL.land: Iceland sits right on the seam where North America and Europe drift apart, about 2 cm a year, half as fast as your fingernails grow. At Þingvellir you can walk in the gap between them.
ISL.people: About 3.9 lakh Icelanders turned all that heat under their feet into a home comfort: nine homes in ten are warmed by hot water piped straight from the ground.
ISL.surprise: There are no mosquitoes. None at all. Scientists still aren't completely sure why.
ISL.scale: You can drive the road all the way round it in about two days. India could hold 32 Icelands, and it has fewer people than Chandigarh.
sources: Wikipedia: Mid-Atlantic Ridge, Þingvellir, Geothermal power in Iceland, Route 1 (Iceland)

CHL.land: Chile runs about 4,300 km from desert to glaciers, but on average it's only about 180 km wide, squeezed between the Andes and the Pacific. On a map it looks less like a country and more like a ribbon.
CHL.people: Most Chileans live in the mild middle, around Santiago. Up north, the Atacama is the driest desert outside the poles: some of its weather stations have never recorded a single drop of rain.
CHL.surprise: Those bone-dry, cloudless nights make it the best stargazing on Earth, which is why so many of the world's biggest telescopes are built here.
CHL.scale: Longer than India is from Kashmir to Kanyakumari, yet on average only a little wider than the drive from Mumbai to Pune.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Chile, Atacama Desert, European Southern Observatory

MNG.land: A high, wind-swept sea of grass, desert and mountains, where winter nights fall below −30°C but the sky stays stubbornly blue. Mongolians call it the Land of the Eternal Blue Sky.
MNG.people: About 36 lakh people live here, the fewest per km² of any country. Nearly half live in Ulaanbaatar, the coldest capital on Earth. Many others still move with their herds, taking their round felt gers with them.
MNG.surprise: At Naadam, the big summer festival, the jockeys in the long-distance horse races are children.
MNG.scale: Almost half the size of India, with roughly as many people as Jaipur.
sources: World Bank: population 2025, area 2024, population density
Wikipedia: Ulaanbaatar, Naadam, Livestock in Mongolia

KEN.land: The equator runs right through Kenya, yet Mount Kenya (5,199 m) still holds small glaciers. Below it, the Great Rift Valley splits the land: a crack where Africa is very slowly tearing itself apart.
KEN.people: The high Rift Valley towns, more than 2,000 m up, have raised many of the world's greatest distance runners. Thin air, strong lungs.
KEN.surprise: Kenya went cashless before most of the world. Since 2007, most adults have paid for things by text message through M-Pesa: chai, school fees, even a cow.
KEN.scale: A bit bigger than Maharashtra and Gujarat put together. India could hold almost six Kenyas.
sources: Wikipedia: Mount Kenya, Great Rift Valley, Iten, M-Pesa

IND.hook: A piece of land that crashed into Asia, and is still pushing.
IND.land: About 50 million years ago, the Indian plate slammed into Asia after a long drift north. The crumple zone is the Himalayas, and the push goes on, about 5 cm a year, so the mountains are still rising.
IND.people: About 146 crore people, more than any other country, speaking hundreds of languages. Every summer the monsoon sets the mood: farms, cricket matches and wedding dates all wait for the rain.
IND.surprise: One country holds both a real desert, the Thar, and one of the wettest places on Earth: Mawsynram in Meghalaya, which gets about 11,800 mm of rain a year.
IND.scale: More than one in every six people on Earth lives here. Driving from Kashmir to Kanyakumari takes about four days.
sources: Wikipedia: Indian Plate, Himalayas, Mawsynram, Thar Desert

USA.hook: A rainforest, a desert, tundra and live volcanoes, under one flag.
USA.land: From Alaska's tundra to Hawaii's volcanoes, with the Rockies, the Great Plains and the Mississippi in between. The plains are a weather highway: icy Arctic air crashes into warm, wet air from the Gulf, which is why it gets more tornadoes than anywhere else.
USA.people: About 34 crore people, most of them descended from someone who arrived from somewhere else. Even today, about 1 in 7 was born in another country.
USA.surprise: Alaska is the most northern, the most western and, thanks to islands that cross the 180° line, also the most eastern state of all.
USA.scale: About three times the size of India. Flying from New York to Los Angeles takes about as long as Delhi to Singapore.
sources: Wikipedia: Tornadoes in the United States, Aleutian Islands

CHN.hook: Land for five time zones, running on a single clock.
CHN.land: China steps down like a giant staircase: the Tibetan Plateau, the roof of the world, at the top; then basins and mountains; then the flat, crowded east, where great rivers like the Yangtze, Asia's longest, reach the sea.
CHN.people: About 141 crore people, and more than 9 in 10 of them live east of a line drawn from the far north-east to the south-west, on less than half of the land.
CHN.surprise: Because the whole country keeps Beijing time, winter sunrise in the far west can come after 9:30 in the morning.
CHN.scale: Almost the same size as the United States, and about three times India. One clock for all of it.
sources: Wikipedia: Time in China, Heihe–Tengchong Line, Yangtze

JPN.hook: Volcanic islands that shake, steam, and still run on time.
JPN.land: About 14,000 islands strung along the Ring of Fire, where four tectonic plates meet. Around a tenth of the world's active volcanoes are here, and the ground trembles somewhere almost every day.
JPN.people: About 12 crore people, mostly squeezed onto narrow coastal plains, because around three-quarters of the land is mountains. Hot springs, called onsen, bubble up all over, warmed by those same volcanoes.
JPN.surprise: The bullet trains, the Shinkansen, have carried billions of passengers since 1964, and their average delay is under a minute.
JPN.scale: A bit bigger than Rajasthan. Tokyo to Osaka, about 500 km, takes about two and a half hours by bullet train.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Japan, Volcanoes of Japan, Shinkansen

GBR.hook: As far north as Canada's prairies, yet green and mild all year.
GBR.land: These islands sit as far north as Canada's cold prairies, but warm water flowing up from the tropics keeps the winters mild and the fields famously green. Famously wet, too.
GBR.people: About 7 crore people in four nations, England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, that share one country, one king and four football teams.
GBR.surprise: Nowhere here is more than about 120 km from the sea.
GBR.scale: Almost exactly the size of Uttar Pradesh, with less than a third of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Climate of the United Kingdom, North Atlantic Current, Coton in the Elms

FRA.hook: Three seas, the Alps, and more cheeses than days in the year.
FRA.land: The mainland touches the Atlantic, the English Channel and the Mediterranean, and climbs to Mont Blanc (4,806 m), the highest peak in the Alps.
FRA.people: About 6.9 crore people, and visitors outnumber them: it's the most visited country on Earth, with around 10 crore tourists a year.
FRA.surprise: Thanks to islands scattered across the oceans, France has more time zones than any other country: 12.
FRA.scale: The mainland is about one-sixth the size of India. Paris to the Mediterranean by fast train takes about three hours.
sources: Wikipedia: Mont Blanc, Tourism in France, Time in France

DEU.hook: Where the Alps slide all the way down to the North Sea.
DEU.land: The land drops from the Alps in the south, through forests and river valleys, to the flat coasts of the North Sea and the Baltic. The Rhine runs through it, and the Danube begins in its Black Forest.
DEU.people: About 8.3 crore people, the most of any country in the European Union. Bread is serious business here: more than 3,000 kinds are officially registered.
DEU.surprise: Long stretches of its motorways, the Autobahn, still have no speed limit at all.
DEU.scale: About the size of Rajasthan, and with roughly as many people too.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Germany, Danube, German bread, Autobahn

BRA.hook: Home to a forest so big it makes its own rain.
BRA.land: About 60% of the Amazon rainforest grows here. Its trees breathe out so much water vapour that they form flying rivers in the sky, carrying rain thousands of kilometres south to farms and cities.
BRA.people: About 21 crore people, most along the Atlantic coast, far from the forest. It's the only country in the Americas where Portuguese is the main language.
BRA.surprise: The Amazon River carries more water to the sea than the next seven biggest rivers put together.
BRA.scale: About two and a half times the size of India, and it borders every South American country except Chile and Ecuador.
sources: Wikipedia: Amazon rainforest, Flying rivers, Amazon River

AUS.hook: An island continent that drifted alone for millions of years.
AUS.land: The flattest and driest continent where people live. Its red centre, the Outback, is ringed by beaches, rainforest and, off the north-east coast, the Great Barrier Reef, the largest structure built by living things.
AUS.people: About 2.8 crore people, and almost 9 in 10 live within 50 km of the sea. The middle is mostly empty, hot and beautiful.
AUS.surprise: Tens of millions of years on its own gave it animals found nowhere else, like the koala and the platypus, a mammal that lays eggs.
AUS.scale: Almost two and a half times the size of India, with fewer people than the Delhi metro area.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Australia, Great Barrier Reef, Platypus

CAN.hook: The second-biggest country, with more lakes than the rest combined.
CAN.land: Ice sheets scraped this land almost bare in the last Ice Age, leaving behind an ancient rock shield, an endless evergreen forest and millions of lakes.
CAN.people: About 4.2 crore people, and most of them live within about 160 km of the US border, where the weather is kindest.
CAN.surprise: It has the longest coastline of any country, more than 2 lakh km: enough to wrap around the Earth five times.
CAN.scale: Almost five times the size of India, with fewer people than Tamil Nadu.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Canada, Canadian Shield, List of countries by length of coastline

RUS.hook: So wide that bedtime in one corner is breakfast in another.
RUS.land: The biggest country on Earth spans 11 time zones, from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific. Most of it is Siberia: endless forest, frozen ground and Lake Baikal, the deepest lake in the world.
RUS.people: About 14 crore people, and about three in four of them live in the west, on the European side of the Ural Mountains.
RUS.surprise: Lake Baikal holds about a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on Earth's surface, more than all five of North America's Great Lakes together.
RUS.scale: More than five times the size of India. The train from Moscow to Vladivostok takes about a week.
sources: Wikipedia: Time in Russia, Lake Baikal, Trans-Siberian Railway

ITA.hook: A boot kicking into the Mediterranean, with volcanoes for laces.
ITA.land: Mostly mountains and hills: the Alps across the top and the Apennines down the spine. Etna and Vesuvius make it Europe's volcano country, and Stromboli has been erupting almost non-stop for over 2,000 years.
ITA.people: About 5.9 crore people, in towns stacked on hilltops and along the coasts. It has more UNESCO World Heritage Sites than any other country.
ITA.surprise: Two whole countries fit inside it: Vatican City and San Marino.
ITA.scale: About the size of Maharashtra, and roughly 1,200 km from the Alps to the toe of the boot.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Italy, Stromboli, World Heritage Sites by country

EGY.hook: Almost everyone lives on a thin green ribbon through the desert.
EGY.land: About 95% of the land is desert. Cutting through it is the Nile, by most counts the longest river on Earth, which fans out into a wide green delta before it reaches the Mediterranean.
EGY.people: About 12 crore people, and around 95% of them live along the Nile and its delta, on roughly 5% of the land.
EGY.surprise: The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest building on Earth for about 3,800 years.
EGY.scale: About a third the size of India. The Nile's journey to the sea is about as far as Delhi to London.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Egypt, Nile, Great Pyramid of Giza

NPL.hook: Eight of the world's ten highest mountains, in a country barely 200 km wide.
NPL.land: It rises from the flat, hot Terai, about 60 m above the sea, to the top of Everest at 8,849 m, all in less than 200 km.
NPL.people: About 3 crore people, many in terraced hill villages. The Kathmandu Valley alone has seven monument zones on UNESCO's World Heritage list.
NPL.surprise: Its flag isn't a rectangle: it's two stacked triangles, the only national flag of its kind.
NPL.scale: A bit smaller than Odisha, and almost exactly the size of Bangladesh, with about a sixth of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Nepal, Mount Everest, Kathmandu Valley, Flag of Nepal

LKA.hook: A teardrop-shaped island of tea, elephants and cinnamon.
LKA.land: It rises from palm-lined beaches to misty central hills, where tea gardens cover the slopes. It's one of the best places on Earth to see wild Asian elephants, and blue whales swim off its southern coast.
LKA.people: About 2.2 crore people. In the hills they pick tea; down south, a few fishermen still fish perched on wooden stilts in the surf.
LKA.surprise: True cinnamon comes from here: most of the world's Ceylon cinnamon still grows on the island.
LKA.scale: About half the size of Tamil Nadu. India could hold 50 of them.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Sri Lanka, Stilt fishing, Cinnamomum verum

PAK.hook: Where three of the world's mightiest mountain ranges meet.
PAK.land: In the far north, the Himalaya, the Karakoram and the Hindu Kush meet, and K2 (8,611 m), the second-highest peak on Earth, stands guard. From there the Indus flows south through deserts and plains to the Arabian Sea.
PAK.people: About 25 crore people, the fifth-most of any country, many farming the Indus plains with one of the largest canal networks in the world.
PAK.surprise: The Karakoram Highway climbs to about 4,700 m at the Khunjerab Pass, one of the highest paved border crossings anywhere.
PAK.scale: About a quarter the size of India, with more people than Brazil.
sources: Wikipedia: K2, Indus River, Indus Basin Irrigation System, Khunjerab Pass

BGD.hook: Where the Ganga and the Brahmaputra finally meet the sea.
BGD.land: Most of the land is the biggest river delta on Earth, built from mud carried down from the Himalayas. Much of it lies less than 10 m above the sea, and rivers can change course from one year to the next.
BGD.people: About 17.6 crore people on a piece of land the size of Nepal, one of the most crowded countries on Earth. Boats are as normal as buses.
BGD.surprise: The Sundarbans, shared with India, is the largest mangrove forest on Earth, and its tigers swim between the islands.
BGD.scale: Almost exactly the size of Nepal, with six times as many people.
sources: Wikipedia: Ganges Delta, Geography of Bangladesh, Sundarbans

IDN.hook: More than 17,000 islands, strung along the equator.
IDN.land: The islands stretch more than 5,000 km along the equator, and sit right on the Ring of Fire: it has more active volcanoes than any other country.
IDN.people: About 28.6 crore people, more than half of them on one island, Java, speaking over 700 languages between them.
IDN.surprise: Komodo dragons, the biggest lizards on Earth, live in the wild only on a handful of its islands.
IDN.scale: Its islands stretch further than Delhi is from Moscow. Together they add up to a bit more than half the size of India.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Indonesia, List of volcanoes in Indonesia, Java, Komodo dragon

ZAF.hook: A country with three capital cities.
ZAF.land: It sits at the southern tip of Africa, where the Atlantic and Indian Oceans meet near Cape Agulhas. Inland, a high grassy plateau, the Highveld, ends at the dramatic cliffs of the Drakensberg.
ZAF.people: About 6.5 crore people and 12 official languages, one of them sign language. Pretoria runs the government, Cape Town makes the laws, and Bloemfontein hears appeals.
ZAF.surprise: Table Mountain, above Cape Town, is one of the oldest mountains on Earth, around six times older than the Himalayas.
ZAF.scale: A little over a third the size of India.
sources: Wikipedia: Cape Agulhas, Languages of South Africa, Table Mountain

MEX.hook: Where corn and chillies were first farmed, and chocolate was first drunk.
MEX.land: High plateaus between two mountain ranges, with deserts in the north and rainforest in the south. The capital is built on an old lake bed, and parts of it sink by tens of centimetres a year.
MEX.people: About 13 crore people, the largest Spanish-speaking population in the world.
MEX.surprise: In the Yucatán, thousands of cenotes, sinkholes of clear blue water, trace the rim of the crater left by the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs.
MEX.scale: About 60% of the size of India. Its capital sits about 2,240 m up, as high as Ooty.
sources: Wikipedia: Maize, Chili pepper, History of chocolate, Mexico City, Cenote, Chicxulub crater

SAU.hook: One of the biggest countries on Earth without a single permanent river.
SAU.land: Most of the land is desert, including the Rub' al Khali, the Empty Quarter, the largest continuous sand desert in the world, where dunes can stand more than 250 m tall.
SAU.people: About 3.7 crore people, mostly in cities like Riyadh and Jeddah. Much of their water comes from the sea: it's one of the world's biggest makers of desalinated water.
SAU.surprise: With all that desert, it has still bought camels from Australia, home to the world's biggest herd of wild camels.
SAU.scale: About two-thirds the size of India, with roughly as many people as Kerala.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Saudi Arabia, Rub' al Khali, Desalination, Australian feral camel

ARE.hook: Pearl-diving villages in living memory, the world's tallest tower today.
ARE.land: Seven emirates on the edge of the Arabian Desert, with mangrove coasts and red dunes inland. Summer days often climb past 45°C.
ARE.people: About 1.2 crore people, and almost 9 in 10 of them came from other countries, more from India than from anywhere else.
ARE.surprise: The Burj Khalifa is 828 m tall. Watch the sunset from the ground, ride up fast enough, and you can watch it set again.
ARE.scale: A little bigger than West Bengal, with about a tenth of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Emirates of the United Arab Emirates, Demographics of the United Arab Emirates, Burj Khalifa

SGP.hook: A city that is also a country, and keeps getting bigger.
SGP.land: One main island and around 60 small ones at the tip of the Malay Peninsula. By piling sand into the sea, it has grown about a quarter bigger since the 1960s.
SGP.people: About 61 lakh people, with four official languages: English, Malay, Mandarin and Tamil.
SGP.surprise: Almost half of it is green: parks, nature reserves and gardens are threaded right through the city.
SGP.scale: About half the size of Delhi. You can drive across it in under an hour.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Singapore, Land reclamation in Singapore, Languages of Singapore

KOR.hook: Seven-tenths mountains, and some of the fastest internet on Earth.
KOR.land: The southern half of a peninsula, wrapped by sea on three sides, with more than 3,000 islands off its coasts. About 70% of it is hills and mountains.
KOR.people: About 5.2 crore people, and around half of them live in and around Seoul.
KOR.surprise: Until 2023, people here counted themselves one year old on the day they were born, and everyone got a year older together on New Year's Day.
KOR.scale: A little bigger than Bihar, with less than half its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of South Korea, Seoul Capital Area, East Asian age reckoning

THA.hook: The only country in Southeast Asia never ruled by a European power.
THA.land: Its shape is often compared to an elephant's head, with the long southern peninsula as the trunk. Hills in the north, rice plains along the Chao Phraya in the middle, and beaches on two seas in the south.
THA.people: About 7.2 crore people, more than 9 in 10 of them Buddhist, with around 40,000 temples.
THA.surprise: Bangkok's full ceremonial name is one of the longest place names on Earth, 168 letters in English. Thais simply call it Krung Thep, the City of Angels.
THA.scale: About the size of Maharashtra and Gujarat together, with roughly as many people as Gujarat.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Thailand, Buddhism in Thailand, Bangkok

TUR.hook: One foot in Europe, the other in Asia.
TUR.land: The Bosphorus strait splits Istanbul in two, with Europe on one shore and Asia on the other. Most of the land is Anatolia, a high plateau where wind and volcanic ash carved the fairy chimneys of Cappadocia.
TUR.people: About 8.6 crore people. Istanbul alone, with about 1.6 crore, has more people than most countries.
TUR.surprise: Göbekli Tepe, a ring of carved stone pillars in the south-east, is about 11,000 years old: older than Stonehenge and the pyramids, and built by hunter-gatherers before farming took hold.
TUR.scale: A bit more than twice the size of Rajasthan. India could hold about four of them.

IRN.hook: Ancient underground canals that still carry water across a dry plateau.
IRN.land: Most of it is a high plateau ringed by the Zagros and Alborz mountains, with two great salt deserts in the middle. Damavand, a sleeping volcano near Tehran, rises to about 5,600 m.
IRN.people: About 9.2 crore people. To farm the dry land, Persians dug qanats: gently sloping tunnels that carry groundwater from the hills for kilometres, without a single pump.
IRN.surprise: The Lut Desert has some of the hottest ground on Earth: satellites have measured its surface at over 70°C.
IRN.scale: About half the size of India, or five Rajasthans.
sources: Wikipedia: Mount Damavand, Qanat, Lut Desert

ESP.hook: A sun-baked plateau where dinner starts at ten at night.
ESP.land: The middle is the Meseta, a high, dry plateau with Madrid almost exactly at its centre. Mountains wall it in, and far away off Africa, the Canary Islands hold Teide, its highest peak, at 3,715 m.
ESP.people: About 4.9 crore people who eat late: lunch around two, dinner often after nine. The clocks are partly to blame: it keeps Central European time, though it sits as far west as Britain.
ESP.surprise: It grows about 40% of all the world's olive oil.
ESP.scale: Almost exactly the size of Maharashtra and Gujarat together.
sources: Wikipedia: Meseta Central, Teide, Time in Spain, Olive oil

GRC.hook: About 6,000 islands, and fewer than 250 of them have people.
GRC.land: Mountains cover most of the mainland, and the Aegean and Ionian seas are scattered with islands, from big Crete to rocks with a single chapel. Earthquakes are common: the African plate is sliding underneath.
GRC.people: About 1 crore people. Their ancestors gave the world the Olympic Games, theatre, democracy and the word geography: geo for Earth, graphy for writing.
GRC.surprise: Mount Olympus, home of the old Greek gods, is a real mountain, 2,918 m high, and you can hike to the top.
GRC.scale: Almost exactly the size of Tamil Nadu, with about a seventh of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Greece, Mount Olympus

NGA.hook: One in every six Africans lives here.
NGA.land: From mangrove swamps on the Atlantic coast, through rainforest and savanna, to the edge of the Sahara in the north. The Niger and Benue rivers meet in the middle in a giant Y.
NGA.people: About 24 crore people speaking more than 500 languages. Lagos, on the coast, is one of the biggest cities in Africa.
NGA.surprise: Its film industry, Nollywood, makes more films every year than Hollywood. Only Bollywood makes more.
NGA.scale: India could hold three and a half of them, yet it has more people than Brazil.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Nigeria, Languages of Nigeria, Nollywood

ARG.hook: Tropical waterfalls at the top, penguins and glaciers at the bottom.
ARG.land: It stretches about 3,700 km from the hot north to Tierra del Fuego. In between lie the flat, fertile Pampas and the Andes, where Aconcagua (6,961 m) is the highest mountain outside Asia.
ARG.people: About 4.6 crore people, about a third of them in and around Buenos Aires. Out on the Pampas, cowboys called gauchos still herd cattle, and steak is close to a national religion.
ARG.surprise: Iguazú Falls, on the border with Brazil, is a curtain of about 275 separate waterfalls.
ARG.scale: The eighth-biggest country on Earth, about 85% of the size of India.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Argentina, Aconcagua, Iguazu Falls

VNM.hook: A long S-shaped coast, with a rice basket at each end.
VNM.land: It curves about 1,650 km along the sea. People say it looks like a carrying pole with a rice basket at each end: the Red River delta in the north and the Mekong delta in the south.
VNM.people: About 10 crore people, and one of the world's biggest growers of rice and coffee. The coffee often comes with sweet condensed milk, or even whipped egg.
VNM.surprise: Son Doong, properly explored only in 2009, is the biggest cave passage on Earth, with its own jungle and clouds inside.
VNM.scale: Almost exactly the size of Rajasthan.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Vietnam, Vietnamese coffee, Hang Sơn Đoòng

MYS.hook: One country in two halves, with the sea in between.
MYS.land: Half sits on the Malay Peninsula, the other half on the island of Borneo. Its rainforests are about 130 million years old, among the oldest on Earth, and home to orangutans.
MYS.people: About 3.6 crore people of Malay, Chinese, Indian and many indigenous roots, which is why breakfast might be nasi lemak, dim sum or roti canai.
MYS.surprise: Rafflesia, the biggest single flower on Earth, grows in its forests: up to a metre across, and it smells of rotting meat.
MYS.scale: About the size of Rajasthan, with fewer than half as many people.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Malaysia, Taman Negara, Rafflesia

PHL.hook: More than 7,600 islands, and a coastline that never seems to end.
PHL.land: Volcanic islands on the Ring of Fire, right in the path of Pacific typhoons: about 20 come its way in a typical year.
PHL.people: About 11.7 crore people, and around a tenth of them live or work abroad. The money they send home keeps many families going.
PHL.surprise: The rice terraces of Ifugao, carved by hand into steep mountainsides, are still farmed today and are a World Heritage Site.
PHL.scale: A little smaller than Maharashtra, with a little fewer people.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of the Philippines, Typhoons in the Philippines, Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras

PER.hook: Where the Inca built a city in the clouds.
PER.land: Three worlds side by side: a bone-dry desert coast, the high Andes, and the Amazon rainforest, which covers about 60% of the land.
PER.people: About 3.5 crore people. High in the Andes, many still speak Quechua, the language of the Inca, and farm thousands of kinds of potato.
PER.surprise: The Nazca Lines, giant drawings of animals scratched into the desert about 2,000 years ago, are best seen from a plane.
PER.scale: About two-fifths the size of India. Lima to Cusco is about an hour by plane, or about 20 hours by bus.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Peru, Quechua languages, Potato, Nazca Lines

COL.hook: The only South American country with coasts on two oceans.
COL.land: The Andes split into three ranges here, with hot valleys in between, then fall away to the Amazon and to the grasslands of the Llanos.
COL.people: About 5.3 crore people. Thanks to all those different heights, its farms grow coffee, flowers, bananas and cacao, sometimes a few hours' drive apart.
COL.surprise: It has more kinds of birds than any other country: around 1,900 species.
COL.scale: About a third the size of India.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Colombia, List of birds of Colombia

MAR.hook: Africa's corner, just 14 km from Europe.
MAR.land: The snowy Atlas Mountains cut across the middle, with Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts on one side and the Sahara on the other.
MAR.people: About 3.8 crore people. Old cities like Fes and Marrakesh are mazes of narrow lanes, and one leather tannery in Fes has been working for nearly a thousand years.
MAR.surprise: The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fes, founded in 859, is often called the oldest university in the world that is still running.
MAR.scale: About one and a third times the size of Rajasthan. India could hold about seven of them.
sources: Wikipedia: Strait of Gibraltar, Atlas Mountains, Chouara Tannery, University of al-Qarawiyyin

ETH.hook: A country with its own calendar, about seven years behind.
ETH.land: A high plateau, the roof of Africa, split by the Great Rift Valley. The Blue Nile starts at Lake Tana, and the Danakil Depression, far below sea level, is one of the hottest places on Earth.
ETH.people: About 13.5 crore people, the most of any landlocked country. Coffee comes from here: legend says a goatherd noticed his goats dancing after nibbling the berries.
ETH.surprise: Lucy, one of the most famous early human ancestors, about 3.2 million years old, was found in its desert in 1974.
ETH.scale: About a third the size of India.
sources: Wikipedia: Ethiopian Highlands, Danakil Depression, Ethiopian calendar, Lucy (Australopithecus)

TZA.hook: Home to Africa's highest mountain and shores of its biggest lake.
TZA.land: Kilimanjaro (5,895 m) rises alone from the plains, snow-capped near the equator. Lake Victoria lies in the north, and Lake Tanganyika, one of the deepest lakes on Earth, in the west.
TZA.people: About 7 crore people speaking more than 100 languages, held together by Swahili. Zanzibar, off the coast, was once the spice island of the Indian Ocean, famous for cloves.
TZA.surprise: Every year, about 15 lakh wildebeest march through the Serengeti in the Great Migration, chased by lions and crocodiles.
TZA.scale: India could hold three and a half of them. Kilimanjaro is more than 1,000 m taller than anything in the Alps.
sources: Wikipedia: Mount Kilimanjaro, Lake Tanganyika, Zanzibar, Serengeti

NZL.hook: One of the last big lands on Earth that people reached.
NZL.land: Two main islands: the volcanic North, with geysers and bubbling mud, and the South, with the Southern Alps and glaciers that slide almost down to the rainforest.
NZL.people: About 53 lakh people, with Māori culture woven through daily life. Polynesian voyagers reached these islands only around 700 years ago.
NZL.surprise: There are four or five sheep for every person: about 2.3 crore sheep in all.
NZL.scale: A little bigger than Uttar Pradesh, with fewer people than Bengaluru.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of New Zealand, Māori people, Sheep farming in New Zealand

NOR.hook: A coastline so wrinkled with fjords it could wrap around the Earth twice.
NOR.land: Glaciers carved deep fjords into the west coast. In the far north, the sun doesn't set for weeks in summer, and the Northern Lights fill the winter sky.
NOR.people: About 56 lakh people. Oil found under the North Sea in 1969 paid for one of the biggest savings funds in the world, owned by everyone in the country.
NOR.surprise: About nine in every ten new cars sold here are electric, the highest share anywhere.
NOR.scale: Almost twice the size of Rajasthan, with fewer people than Hyderabad.
sources: Wikipedia: Fjords of Norway, Midnight sun, Government Pension Fund of Norway, Plug-in electric vehicles in Norway

SWE.hook: Forests, almost a lakh lakes, and the right to camp almost anywhere.
SWE.land: A long land of forests, which cover about 70% of it, and nearly a lakh lakes, reaching north into the Arctic.
SWE.people: About 1.1 crore people, with a right called allemansrätten: anyone may walk, camp and pick berries on almost any land, as long as they're careful.
SWE.surprise: Every winter, at Jukkasjärvi in the far north, a hotel is built from blocks of river ice. Every spring, it melts back into the river.
SWE.scale: About one and a half times the size of Rajasthan, with fewer people than Delhi.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Sweden, Freedom to roam, Icehotel

FIN.hook: Called the land of a thousand lakes; it actually has about 1.9 lakh.
FIN.land: Flat and forested, scraped smooth by Ice Age glaciers, with about 1.9 lakh lakes and tens of thousands of islands. In Lapland, the far north, the winter sun barely rises for weeks.
FIN.people: About 56 lakh people and around 30 lakh saunas, roughly one for every two people.
FIN.surprise: It has topped the World Happiness Report as the happiest country on Earth every year since 2018.
FIN.scale: Almost exactly the size of Rajasthan, with fewer people than Pune.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Finland, Sauna, World Happiness Report

NLD.hook: About a quarter of it lies below sea level, held back by dikes.
NLD.land: Flat as a table and criss-crossed by canals, dikes and dunes. Windmills once pumped the water out; today, pumping stations keep the land dry.
NLD.people: About 1.8 crore people, and more bicycles than people: around 2.3 crore of them.
NLD.surprise: Flevoland, a whole province, was pumped dry from the sea in the 1900s. It's one of the biggest artificial islands on Earth.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of the Netherlands, Cycling in the Netherlands, Flevoland

CHE.hook: Mountains everywhere, and four national languages.
CHE.land: The Alps cover about 60% of it, with glaciers, deep lakes and more than 40 peaks above 4,000 m.
CHE.people: About 91 lakh people speaking German, French, Italian or Romansh, depending on the valley. Big decisions often go to a public vote, several times a year.
CHE.surprise: The Gotthard Base Tunnel, 57 km long, is the longest railway tunnel in the world, running right under the Alps.
CHE.scale: About the size of Kerala, with about a quarter of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Switzerland, Languages of Switzerland, Gotthard Base Tunnel

PRT.hook: A small country that once sailed to every corner of the world.
PRT.land: A narrow strip on the Atlantic edge of Europe, plus the islands of Madeira and the Azores far out at sea. The north is green and wet, the south sunny and dry.
PRT.people: About 1.1 crore people. In 1498, Vasco da Gama sailed from here to Kozhikode, the first sea voyage from Europe to India.
PRT.surprise: It produces about half of the world's cork, peeled from the bark of cork oaks without cutting the trees down.
PRT.scale: Almost exactly the size of Bihar, with about a twelfth of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Portugal, Vasco da Gama, Cork (material)

IRL.hook: So green and so rainy it's called the Emerald Isle.
IRL.land: A saucer-shaped island: low green plains in the middle, ringed by hills and wild Atlantic cliffs like the Cliffs of Moher, about 200 m high.
IRL.people: About 55 lakh people, yet around 7 crore people across the world claim Irish roots, more than ten times as many.
IRL.surprise: There are no wild snakes. Legend credits Saint Patrick; scientists credit the Ice Age and the sea.
IRL.scale: A little smaller than Assam, with fewer people than Chennai.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Ireland, Cliffs of Moher, Irish diaspora, Snakes in Ireland

POL.hook: Flat fields, sand dunes, and Europe's last wild bison.
POL.land: Mostly flat plains, which may be where the name comes from: pole means field. The Tatra Mountains rise in the south, and the Baltic coast has some of Europe's biggest moving sand dunes.
POL.people: About 3.6 crore people. Warsaw's old town was almost totally destroyed in the Second World War, then rebuilt brick by brick using old paintings and drawings.
POL.surprise: In Białowieża Forest, one of Europe's last old-growth forests, wild European bison roam free. They were saved from extinction here.
POL.scale: About the size of Madhya Pradesh, with less than half its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Poland, Słowiński National Park, Warsaw Old Town, Białowieża Forest

UKR.hook: Some of the richest farmland on Earth, the black soil of the steppe.
UKR.land: Mostly wide, fertile plains, the steppe, with the Carpathian Mountains in the west and the Black Sea in the south. The Dnipro river runs right through the middle.
UKR.people: Its black soil, called chernozem, is so rich that it has long been known as the breadbasket of Europe, growing wheat, corn and sunflowers.
UKR.surprise: Arsenalna, a station on the Kyiv metro, is one of the deepest in the world, about 105 m underground.
UKR.scale: A bit less than twice the size of Rajasthan. India could hold about five of them.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Ukraine, Chernozem, Arsenalna (Kyiv Metro)

AFG.hook: Where the Hindu Kush meets the old Silk Road.
AFG.land: Mountains cover most of it. The Hindu Kush runs through the middle, with peaks above 7,000 m, and the long, narrow Wakhan Corridor reaches all the way to China.
AFG.people: About 4.4 crore people, many in mountain valleys. For centuries, Silk Road caravans crossed here, carrying silk, spices and ideas between India, Persia and China.
AFG.surprise: Band-e-Amir, a chain of six lakes high in the mountains, is an unreal deep blue, held back by natural walls of mineral.
AFG.scale: About a fifth of the size of India.
sources: Wikipedia: Hindu Kush, Wakhan Corridor, Silk Road, Band-e-Amir National Park

MMR.hook: A land of golden pagodas, with thousands of temples on one plain.
MMR.land: The Irrawaddy river runs almost the whole length of the country, from Himalayan foothills in the north to a wide, green delta in the south.
MMR.people: About 5.5 crore people, most of them Buddhist. On the plain of Bagan, more than 2,000 old temples and pagodas still stand.
MMR.surprise: On Inle Lake, fishermen row standing on one leg, with the other wrapped around the oar, leaving their hands free for the nets.
MMR.scale: About a fifth of the size of India, just across the hills from India's north-east.
sources: Wikipedia: Irrawaddy River, Bagan, Inle Lake

MDV.hook: The flattest country on Earth, barely above the waves.
MDV.land: About 1,200 coral islands grouped into 26 atolls, scattered across the Indian Ocean. The highest natural point is only about 2.4 m above the sea.
MDV.people: About 5.3 lakh people live on around 200 of the islands; many others are resorts. Fish, mostly tuna, is on almost every plate.
MDV.surprise: On some beaches, the waves glow blue at night, lit up by tiny plankton.
MDV.scale: All its land adds up to about a fifth of Delhi, scattered across more than 800 km of ocean.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of the Maldives, Bioluminescence

QAT.hook: A thumb of desert sticking out into the Gulf.
QAT.land: A flat, low peninsula of sand and gravel. In the south, tall dunes run straight into the sea at Khor Al Adaid, the Inland Sea.
QAT.people: About 30 lakh people, and only around one in eight is a citizen: most came to work, many of them from India.
QAT.surprise: It sits on one of the largest natural gas fields on Earth, which made it one of the richest countries per person.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Qatar, Khor Al Adaid, Demographics of Qatar, South Pars/North Dome Gas-Condensate field

ISR.hook: A dry land that taught the world to water plants drop by drop.
ISR.land: A narrow land between the Mediterranean and the Jordan Valley: a green coast in the north, the Negev desert across much of the south, and the Sea of Galilee, about 200 m below sea level.
ISR.people: About 1 crore people. With little rain, farmers here developed modern drip irrigation, now used on farms all over the world, including in India.
ISR.surprise: It recycles almost 90% of its waste water for farming, more than any other country.
ISR.scale: About the size of Manipur, with about three times as many people.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Israel, Negev, Sea of Galilee, Drip irrigation, Water supply and sanitation in Israel

JOR.hook: Home to the lowest dry land on Earth, the shore of the Dead Sea.
JOR.land: Mostly desert, with a deep rift valley running down its western edge. The Dead Sea, shared with its neighbours, is so salty that you float without even trying.
JOR.people: About 1.2 crore people. In the south, the Nabataeans carved Petra, a whole city of tombs and temples, straight into pink sandstone cliffs about 2,000 years ago.
JOR.surprise: Wadi Rum's red desert looks so much like another planet that it has stood in for Mars in films.
JOR.scale: Almost exactly the size of West Bengal, with about a ninth of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Dead Sea, Petra, Wadi Rum

KAZ.hook: The biggest landlocked country on Earth.
KAZ.land: Mostly a vast, flat steppe of grass and desert, with snowy mountains in the south-east and a long shore on the Caspian Sea in the west.
KAZ.people: About 2.1 crore people. Apples first grew wild here: the old name of its biggest city, Alma-Ata, roughly means father of apples.
KAZ.surprise: Baikonur, in its desert, was the world's first space launch site: Yuri Gagarin blasted off from here in 1961.
KAZ.scale: About four-fifths the size of India, with fewer people than the Delhi metro area.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Kazakhstan, Malus sieversii, Almaty, Baikonur Cosmodrome

UZB.hook: One of only two double-landlocked countries on Earth.
UZB.land: Desert and steppe, watered by two great rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya. The Aral Sea, once one of the biggest lakes on Earth, has mostly dried up since the rivers were drained for cotton.
UZB.people: About 3.7 crore people. Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva, blue-tiled Silk Road cities, have been trading for more than 2,000 years.
UZB.surprise: In Muynak, rusting fishing boats sit stranded in the sand, many kilometres from where the Aral Sea's shore is now.
UZB.scale: About one and a third times the size of Rajasthan.
sources: Wikipedia: Landlocked country, Aral Sea, Samarkand, Moynaq

CUB.hook: A long Caribbean island where 1950s cars still cruise the streets.
CUB.land: The biggest island in the Caribbean, long and narrow, ringed by coral reefs and more than 4,000 smaller islands and cays.
CUB.people: About 1.1 crore people. New cars were hard to get for decades, so many 1950s American cars are still running, kept alive with clever repairs.
CUB.surprise: The bee hummingbird, the smallest bird on Earth at about 5 cm long, lives only here.
CUB.scale: Almost exactly the size of Telangana, with about a third of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Cuba, Yank tank, Bee hummingbird

VEN.hook: Flat-topped mountains rising from the jungle like islands in the sky.
VEN.land: Caribbean beaches in the north, the Andes in the west, the wide grasslands of the Llanos, and in the south, giant flat-topped mountains called tepuis, rising straight out of the jungle.
VEN.people: About 2.9 crore people, living on top of the largest proven oil reserves on Earth.
VEN.surprise: Over Lake Maracaibo, lightning flashes on up to 160 nights a year, more than anywhere else on Earth.
VEN.scale: About 2.7 times the size of Rajasthan. Angel Falls, at 979 m, is almost 20 times as tall as Niagara.
sources: Wikipedia: Tepui, Llanos, Oil reserves in Venezuela, Catatumbo lightning, Angel Falls

BOL.hook: A country with two capitals, both high in the Andes.
BOL.land: The west is the Altiplano, a high plateau about 3,700 m up between two ranges of the Andes; the east drops down to the Amazon and dry forests. Lake Titicaca sits on the border with Peru.
BOL.people: About 1.3 crore people, many speaking Quechua or Aymara. La Paz, where the government sits, is about 3,600 m up; Sucre is the official capital.
BOL.surprise: Salar de Uyuni is the biggest salt flat on Earth, about 10,000 km². After rain it becomes a mirror so perfect that the sky seems to touch the ground.
BOL.scale: About a third the size of India.
sources: Wikipedia: Altiplano, La Paz, Sucre, Salar de Uyuni

ECU.hook: Named after the line that runs right through it: the equator.
ECU.land: The Andes run down the middle, lined with volcanoes like Cotopaxi, with the Pacific coast to the west and the Amazon to the east. About 1,000 km out to sea lie the Galápagos Islands.
ECU.people: About 1.8 crore people. The capital, Quito, sits about 2,850 m up, almost exactly on the equator.
ECU.surprise: Because the Earth bulges at the equator, the top of Chimborazo is the farthest point from Earth's centre, further out than the top of Everest.
ECU.scale: A little bigger than Uttar Pradesh, with less than a tenth of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Ecuador, Galápagos Islands, Quito, Chimborazo

MDG.hook: An island where nine in ten plants and animals live nowhere else.
MDG.land: The fourth-biggest island on Earth. It split off from India about 88 million years ago and has drifted alone in the Indian Ocean ever since.
MDG.people: About 3.3 crore people. Its first settlers sailed all the way from Borneo, and the Malagasy language is still related to languages spoken there.
MDG.surprise: Lemurs, cousins of monkeys with huge eyes, live in the wild almost nowhere else.
MDG.scale: About one and three-quarter times the size of Rajasthan.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Madagascar, Malagasy language, Lemur

GHA.hook: Gold, cocoa, and the biggest man-made lake on Earth by area.
GHA.land: Tropical forest in the south, savanna in the north, and Lake Volta in between, made by a dam in 1965.
GHA.people: About 3.5 crore people. It was the first country south of the Sahara to win independence from colonial rule, in 1957.
GHA.surprise: It's the world's second-biggest grower of cocoa, so a good share of the world's chocolate starts on its farms.
GHA.scale: Almost exactly the size of Uttar Pradesh, with about a seventh of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Lake Volta, History of Ghana, Cocoa production in Ghana

COD.hook: A rainforest second only to the Amazon, and the deepest river on Earth.
COD.land: Most of it is the Congo Basin, the second-biggest rainforest on Earth. The Congo River, the deepest river known, sweeps through it in a giant arc that crosses the equator twice.
COD.people: About 11 crore people speaking more than 200 languages. Kinshasa, the capital, is one of Africa's biggest cities.
COD.surprise: The bonobo, one of our two closest living relatives, lives in the wild only here.
COD.scale: About seven-tenths the size of India, and the second-biggest country in Africa.
sources: Wikipedia: Congo Basin, Congo River, Kinshasa, Bonobo

DZA.hook: Africa's biggest country, and most of it is the Sahara.
DZA.land: A narrow green strip along the Mediterranean, then the Atlas Mountains, then desert for more than four-fifths of the land. Deep in the Sahara rise the volcanic Hoggar Mountains.
DZA.people: About 4.7 crore people, and nearly all of them live in the north, near the coast.
DZA.surprise: Tassili n'Ajjer, a sandstone plateau in the Sahara, holds thousands of rock paintings, some showing giraffes and hippos from a time when the desert was green.
DZA.scale: About seven-tenths the size of India.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Algeria, Hoggar Mountains, Tassili n'Ajjer

KHM.hook: Home to Angkor Wat, the biggest religious monument on Earth.
KHM.land: Flat plains around a great lake, the Tonlé Sap, and the Mekong river. In the rainy season the Mekong swells so much that the Tonlé Sap river turns around and flows backwards, and the lake grows to about five times its size.
KHM.people: About 1.8 crore people, most of them rice farmers. Angkor Wat, built in the 1100s, is on the national flag.
KHM.surprise: Angkor Wat was first built as a Hindu temple to Vishnu, before it became Buddhist.
KHM.scale: A little smaller than Karnataka, with about a quarter of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Tonlé Sap, Angkor Wat, Flag of Cambodia

PRK.hook: One of the most closed-off countries on Earth.
PRK.land: The northern half of the Korean peninsula, and about 80% of it is mountains. Mount Paektu, a volcano with a crater lake, stands on its northern border.
PRK.people: About 2.7 crore people. Few outsiders visit, and few people can leave.
PRK.surprise: In satellite photos at night it is almost completely dark, while its neighbours glow brightly all around it.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of North Korea, Paektu Mountain, Korean peninsula at night

DNK.hook: Nowhere more than about 50 km from the sea.
DNK.land: A low, flat peninsula, Jutland, plus more than 400 named islands. Its highest natural point is only about 171 m above the sea.
DNK.people: About 60 lakh people. In Copenhagen, around half of all commuters arrive by bicycle.
DNK.surprise: LEGO was invented here. The name comes from leg godt, Danish for play well.
DNK.scale: A little smaller than Haryana, with about a fifth of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Denmark, Cycling in Copenhagen, Lego

AUT.hook: About two-thirds Alps, and the home of the waltz.
AUT.land: The Alps cover about two-thirds of it, and the Danube flows across the north, past Vienna. The highest peak, Grossglockner, reaches 3,798 m.
AUT.people: About 92 lakh people. Mozart was born in Salzburg, and Vienna gave the world the waltz and some of its most famous cafés.
AUT.surprise: Hallstatt, a village on an Alpine lake, has been mining salt for about 7,000 years.
AUT.scale: About the size of Jharkhand, with about a quarter of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Austria, Grossglockner, Hallstatt

BEL.hook: Three official languages and very serious chocolate.
BEL.land: Mostly low and flat, with a short North Sea coast, rising to the forested Ardennes hills in the south-east.
BEL.people: About 1.2 crore people who speak Dutch, French or German, depending on where they live. Brussels is home to the main offices of the European Union.
BEL.surprise: Antwerp is one of the world's great diamond centres, and many of its diamond traders have roots in Gujarat.
BEL.scale: Smaller than Kerala, with about a third of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Belgium, Languages of Belgium, Antwerp diamond district

CZE.hook: A bowl of mountains, full of castles.
CZE.land: The western half, Bohemia, is a basin almost completely ringed by low mountains. The Vltava river runs through Prague on its way north.
CZE.people: About 1.1 crore people, who drink more beer per person than anyone else in the world.
CZE.surprise: Prague Castle is one of the biggest old castle complexes on Earth, and there are around 2,000 castles and châteaux across the country.
CZE.scale: About the size of Assam, with about a third of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Bohemia, Beer in the Czech Republic, Prague Castle

HRV.hook: More than a thousand islands along a crescent of coast.
HRV.land: A crescent-shaped country: a long Adriatic coast with more than a thousand islands, and plains along the Danube inland. The Plitvice Lakes are 16 lakes linked by waterfalls.
HRV.people: About 39 lakh people. The necktie comes from here: soldiers' knotted scarves inspired the cravat in 1600s France.
HRV.surprise: Dalmatian dogs are named after Dalmatia, its sunny southern coast.
HRV.scale: Almost exactly the size of West Bengal, with about a twenty-fifth of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Croatia, Plitvice Lakes National Park, Cravat, Dalmatian dog

MUS.hook: A volcanic island where the dodo once lived.
MUS.land: A volcanic island in the Indian Ocean, almost completely ringed by coral reefs, about 2,000 km off the coast of Africa.
MUS.people: About 12 lakh people, and around two-thirds have Indian roots. Their ancestors came in the 1800s, many from Bihar, to work the sugar plantations, and Bhojpuri is still spoken.
MUS.surprise: The dodo, a big flightless bird, lived only here, and was gone within about a hundred years of sailors arriving.
MUS.scale: About one and a third times the size of Delhi, with about a twentieth of its people.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Mauritius, Indo-Mauritians, Dodo

FJI.hook: More than 300 islands, and the 180° line runs right through.
FJI.land: About 330 islands in the South Pacific, around 110 of them lived on. The 180° line of longitude crosses the island of Taveuni.
FJI.people: About 9 lakh people, and nearly two-fifths have Indian roots: their ancestors came to work the sugar plantations from 1879, and a local form of Hindi is widely spoken.
FJI.surprise: Rugby is huge here: its sevens team won Olympic gold in 2016 and again in 2020, the country's first Olympic golds ever.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Fiji, Taveuni, Indo-Fijians, Fiji national rugby sevens team

OMN.hook: A desert country where the monsoon turns the hills green.
OMN.land: Desert mountains, the Hajar, in the north, a long coast on the Arabian Sea, and in the south, Dhofar, where the summer monsoon turns the hills green and misty.
OMN.people: About 55 lakh people. Sailors from here traded with India for thousands of years, and frankincense from the south was carried across the ancient world.
OMN.surprise: Frankincense trees still grow wild in Dhofar, and their sweet-smelling sap has been traded for thousands of years.
OMN.scale: Almost exactly the size of Madhya Pradesh.
sources: Wikipedia: Geography of Oman, Dhofar Governorate, Frankincense
